start.text: Aldous looks up at your face the way he has since you asked him, as if it might come back to him if he caught it unawares.

first.text: Ah. Ah, no. No, no. Not yet. It's too soon for— you should be—
Forgive me. Brother Aldous Wren, of the Keepers of the Spire. Formerly. Currently of this bench.

choice.text: The Long Book's shut, Brother.
Do you know me?
Mara says you can relight the Gull's Beacon.
I've seen the beacon. It wants a memory.
The Gull's Beacon is lit.
I'm ready for the rest of your story.
You said I'd make you talk. So talk.
Hold out your ember. "Look at it, Brother. Then tell me."
Wynn Sallow kept a coal.
Dunstan Tollen walked back out of the fog.
The big man on Mara's stool walked back out of the fog.
Dunstan Tollen walked back out of the fog. He's staying on the fen to turn the boards for whoever comes next.
A Saltmarrow man walked back out of the fog on the fen. He's staying to turn the boards for whoever comes next.
The Provost of Kindleby says she'd send a boat for you.
Look at this, Brother. It came out of the smoke on Kindleby, into my hand.
I went into the fog and came out again not knowing why I'd gone.
What happened at the Hearthspire?
The ferry's come.
Rest easy, Brother.

know_me.text: Know you? I've had a good look since Wynn's novice. You'd think a door-warden would know. I don't.
You asked me that on the bench and I told you the truth. I'm still looking. I'll tell you the day I find it.

spire.text: It went out. Fire does that. Even very old fire.

choice.text: You were there. You don't have to tell me yet.
Nine hundred years, and it just "went out"? Tell me the truth.

spire.text: You're patient with an old coward. I'm working up to it. Truly.
I've said what I'll say on that.

spire_gentle.text: …Thank you. I'll tell you. Not on this bench, not with this cup. But I will.
I can say this much sober: it did not go out by accident.

spire_pressed.text: The truth is a heavier thing than you'd think, Wakebearer. I dropped it once already.
He turns his shoulder to you and stares at the fog until you leave him be.

beacon.text: The Gull's Beacon. Yes. It can be lit. The ember isn't the hard part.
A beacon has to be fed. Not oil — memory. Something the fog left behind. A Remnant.
Whatever you feed it, the island keeps everything else… and loses that one thing for good.
That pebble in your pocket is humming loud enough to wake the Spire. It would do. Gods forgive whoever chooses.
Remnants wash up where the fog thins. That child with the collection of lost things — Pell? — may already hold one.
Go up to the headland. Look at it. Then decide whether you still want to.

after_beacon.text: So you've seen the cradle. Now you know why I'm on this bench.
People will tell you to burn whatever hurts least. There isn't one. There's only whichever you can live with having chosen.
And a Remnant needn't be found. Hold a loved thing in the grey long enough and the memory settles into it. We Keepers knew that trick. We knew it far too well.
Whatever you pick — come and tell me after. I owe you the rest of a story, and I'd like to pay it sober.

beacon_lit.text: I know. I felt it catch from this bench, like a hand on the back of my neck. Nine hundred midwinters, and it still knows how.
The lullaby. That child will sleep worse, and never know why. You chose something small that was everything to someone. They all are.
The founding knot. The village's beginning, for its future. A Keeper's choice — tidy, and cold. I'd have made it too. That's not praise.
Mara's brother. She gave him willingly; I saw her at the gate. That's a kind of courage I never had.
I promised you the rest of a story. The cork's in the bottle, for once. Sit, if you've the time.

choice.text: Sit with him.
Later, Brother.

beacon_lit.text: There are things I should tell you. I'm not brave enough yet. Perhaps you'll make me.

spire_after.text: You've had all of it I can bear to give. The High Keeper put it out, and I held the door.
And something small and bright went down the stair past me. I think about that more than the rest.

confess_gentle.text: He sets the bottle down at the far end of the bench, out of reach, and looks at it the way a man looks at a dog he has told to stay.
I kept the east stair of the Hearthspire. Thirty-one years. Nobody climbs to the flame without a door-warden's say, and on the night of the Snuffing, I was the door.
It didn't gutter. It didn't starve. Fire that has burned nine hundred years doesn't forget how. It was put out — on purpose — by a hand that had every right to tend it.

choice.text: Whose hand?

confess_whose.text: The High Keeper's. Ours. The one of us who climbed highest and knelt closest.

choice.text: Say the name.
Why would the High Keeper do that?

confess_name.text: No. Names carry, in this fog, and that one is heavy enough to sink a boat. Ask me on Cindermoor, if we're ever both standing there.

confess_why.text: Why, I don't know. That's the truth, and it's the worst of it. I held the door and I didn't ask. Three months and a great deal of bad wine, and I still haven't asked.
But I'll tell you the part I never told anyone. Something came down the stair past me that night. Down, not up. A light — small and quick, cupped in someone's hands like a moth. I never saw the face.
His eyes go to your hand, and the ember in it, and away again.
When I first saw you, I said "too soon." The legends are very sure: the flame wakes someone when it fails. And it hadn't failed. It was put out. So what woke you, Wakebearer?

choice.text: I don't know.
Something that lit your beacon. That's enough for now.

confess_unknown.text: No. Nor do I. We'll be two people who don't know, then. There are worse fellowships.

confess_enough.text: Ha. Yes. It'll have to be, won't it.

confess_end.text: If you want more than an old man's word, the answers are where the fire was. The Hearthspire, on Cindermoor.
Nothing crosses to Cindermoor but the Tidewright ferry, and the ferry hasn't run since the Snuffing. Ferrymen won't sail into what they can't see.
With the Gull lit, they'll see Saltmarrow from the water again. Ask Mara when it's due. She knows the Tidewrights' ways better than I know my own order's.
He picks at the faded ember stitched on his sleeve until the threads give, and presses it into your palm.
Take it. I've no right to wear it. Some of my brothers might still open a door for that mark. Most would sooner shut one.

balk.text: Make me? Did I say that? I say a great many things.
You lit a beacon. Lovely. Go and look at what it cost them down at the harbor, and then come and tell me you still want a Keeper's secrets on top.
He tips the bottle up. It's already empty; he keeps it there anyway, until you step back.

confess_grudging.text: You open your hand. He looks at the ember a long time. The light of it moves in his wet eyes.
It didn't go out by accident. It was put out. By the High Keeper. And I was the door-warden on the stair that night, and I let it happen, and I ran.

choice.text: Why did the High Keeper do it?
That's all?

grudging_why.text: That's all you'll have from me. I don't know why. I've spent three months making sure I don't.
If you want more than an old man's word, the answers are where the fire was. The Hearthspire, on Cindermoor.
Nothing crosses to Cindermoor but the Tidewright ferry, and the ferry hasn't run since the Snuffing. Ferrymen won't sail into what they can't see.
With the Gull lit, they'll see Saltmarrow from the water again. Ask Mara when it's due. She knows the Tidewrights' ways better than I know my own order's.
And Wakebearer — whatever you are. You came too soon. Remember I said so.

ferry.text: I heard. I'm not coming, before you ask. A Keeper on a Tidewright deck? They'd weigh me and find me light, and they'd be right.
Keep that sleeve out of sight till Cindermoor. It'll open a door or two there. Not before.
Thornwold had a beacon-keeper of ours, once. I'll not say the name. Names carry. But if someone in those woods looks at your ember like they've seen one before… be kind to them. Kinder than I'd be.

know_me_before.text: Know you? I— no. No. Everyone looks a bit familiar after the fourth cup.
He doesn't meet your eyes. His hand has drifted to cover the faded ember stitched on his sleeve.

novice.note: Saves where the name was said before Day 47 never started the quest.

novice.text: He has the bottle halfway to his mouth. It stops there.
You said it out loud. In this fog. I wouldn't, the day the ferry came. Names carry.
You tell him: the ridge over Thornwold, the bench under the lodge's eave, the iron box and the chisel, a sliver a night, one lantern each. The hood put back.
A sliver a night. That's Wynn. Never took a whole coal down the stair in thirty winters when half would do.
I gave you the bare bones of that night and told you to go. I thought I was the only one of us who ran and lived. Wynn didn't run. Kept the light. Kept it for strangers.
He corks the bottle and sets it down on the slate, carefully, as if it might wake.
I told you there was a keeper of ours in those woods. I didn't tell you I'd counted Wynn among the dead. I've been pouring one out for that coal every night since the ferry.
But you didn't sail two lanes to tell me Wynn's well. What's Wynn sent you to ask?
You tell him: the last midwinter, the east stair, a novice on the landing with a light cupped in their hands. 'Keep one back this year, Keeper Sallow.'

And there's the scale's salt on your palm. I can smell the lane-house on you. A friend of the lanes, asking a Keeper which of his novices said what to whom. My brothers would call that Tidewright business. They'd be right, and I don't care.
The Tidewrights offered you their scale, I'd guess, and you stepped off it. My brothers would like that in you. Don't let that be the reason you did it.
The last midwinter. The coals came down from the flame one keeper at a time, and every one of them past me. I could tell you them in order. I have. Most nights, to this bench.

And on the landings, the novices, holding lights for them to see the steps by. Seven that winter. Ama Rusk, with the cough. Tobin and Kit Petch, who swapped places to fool me and never once did. Joss Merrow, who dropped things. Edda Pike. Fennick, who sang on the steps when he thought nobody could hear.
He stops. He counts on his fingers, under his breath, and comes to the end of them, and starts again.
Six. I know there were seven. Seven lights up and seven down, every night of that winter; I counted them. And on the east landing, where the seventh face should be, there's—
He looks out over the harbor at the grey. He doesn't finish. Your ember beats in your palm, once, slow, like something knocking on the inside of a door.
Thirty-one years, and I never lost a face off that stair. Not one. The fog's had one.

choice.text: Wynn would want to know who it was.
Could it have been me?

novice_lamp.text: So would I. Tell Wynn: the seventh light, on the east landing, and the door-warden's sorry. Tell Wynn I'm sorry for all of it, while you're there. Wynn'll know what I mean.

novice_self.text: He looks at you for a long time. Long enough that the gulls come round twice.
I don't know. That's the worst thing I could say to you, and it's the truth.

I've been looking at your face since the morning you came up off the beach. I can't find it anywhere. Not on the stair. Not off it. A face I'd never seen, I'd know I'd never seen. Yours, I can't tell.
I told you you came too soon. I'm less sure, now, that it's soon at all.

novice_roll.text: There's a roll, at the Spire. Every novice's name, and the day they came up, in the door-warden's hand. Mine, for thirty-one years. It's in the warden's niche at the foot of the east stair, unless somebody's burned it.
If you ever get across to Cindermoor, count the names for that winter. If there are seven, the seventh's yours to read. Whoever's it is.

He gets up off the bench, slowly, joint by joint, and goes to the cold brazier at the Wrens' steps. He takes a stick from the driftwood by the door and lays it across the bowl. Then another, crossways. Then a third.
A door-warden keeps a hearth laid for whoever comes down the stair. I let this one go cold. I've no fire to put to it. But it's laid.

walked_back.text: I know. I watched him come round the breakwater from this bench, rowing the wrong way. I thought it was the drink.
I know. I watched the boat come round the breakwater from this bench, rowing the wrong way. I thought it was the drink.
Nine hundred years the Keepers have said it, every midwinter, to every island that asked us to go and look: the fog doesn't give back what walks into it. What walks in stays walked in.
I said it to Mara. The week he went. She came up those steps and asked me, a Keeper, whether he'd come back, and I said it to her face.
I said it to somebody on this harbor not long since. I can't think who. It doesn't matter who. I said it.
He walked back behind my light.
He walked back behind my light. Now he's laying the boards the other way, so others can.
Then it was a lie. Or it was only true while the Spire burned, and none of us ever asked why that should be.
I don't know which is worse. I'll sit here and find out.
Put it on the list, Wakebearer. It's getting to be a long list.

provost_boat.text: Aldous stops with the bottle halfway to his mouth, and then puts it down on the bench beside him, which you have not seen him do.
Agathe Lorn. Provost, is she. She was Sister Agathe when I was on the stair. She put me on report twice in one winter, and both times I'd earned it.
A boat. For me. To sit in front of the chapter and say it.

Did she ask about the light on the stair? No. She said if I'd seen something. That's Agathe. She'll hear a thing if it's said to her properly, in a room, with the candles lit. She'll not come looking for it.

I came down the east stair with a light going past me and I didn't stop till this bench. I've not been in a boat since the one that brought me. I'll not get in one now to be weighed by a chapter. They'd find me light. They'd be right.

I ran down the east stair and I didn't stop till this bench. I've not been in a boat since the one that brought me. I'll not get in one now to be weighed by a chapter. They'd find me light. They'd be right.

choice.text: Then write it down. I'll carry it to her.
Then don't go.

provost_letter.text: He finds a stub of pencil in his sleeve and tears an old tide-table off the harbor wall behind him. He writes on the back of it slowly, for a long time, with his tongue in the corner of his mouth like a novice, and crosses out, and writes again. Then he folds it twice and writes on the outside.
Don't read it. You'd only be disappointed. It's mostly apologising.
The rest is the stair. All of it. The light going down past me, and which way it went. I've never written it down. It looks smaller, written.
Give it her in her hand. Not on a table. She'll know the difference.

provost_no.text: Tell her— no. Tell her I'm sorry about the reports. She'll know what that means. It means no.
He picks the bottle up again, and looks at it, and doesn't drink.

taper.text: He puts the bottle down without looking where. It finds the slate on its own.

Off my shelf in the niche at the foot of the east stair. I cut them. Thirty-one years, a notch to a landing, the same knife. You'd hand one to a novice lit, and they'd hold it on their landing while the keepers came down with the coals, and if the wind took it they'd count notches with their thumb till they knew where they were.
That one's been burned down past the third landing. Somebody went up a long way with it.
Seven lights up and seven down, I told you. Every night of that winter. And you bring me a taper out of a fire.
You asked me could it have been you. I said I didn't know. I still don't know. I like it less.

I told you a light went down the east stair past me, the night it went dark. Going down, not going out. I didn't tell you the rest, because it's nothing. Whoever carried it was counting. Under their breath, the landings. I heard them counting.
He looks at the taper and not at you.
Don't light it. A taper's for the stair. You'll know which stair.

turned_back.text: He looks at your hand before he looks at you, the way a man checks a lamp's wick before he asks where you've been with it.
But you came out. That's the part to hold on to.

It keeps back off a lit ember. Not far. A boat's length, when it's burning well; you'll have seen it lean away from you, the way it leans off a lantern. When that ring's closing on your boots, the ember's telling you. Turn round then, not after.
And it took the errand and left you the rest? It does that. Takes the newest thing first. A man forgets what he went up the stair for long before he forgets the stair.
It took the errand and left you the rest. The fog takes the newest thing first. I've watched it do the opposite to men, though. You're not a man it does the opposite to.
The books say Isolde Vane's ember walked her out of the grey every time, back to where she'd last stood clear. They don't say how it knew the way. Nobody ever wrote down what an ember knows.
He goes back to his slate. After a while: "Don't make a habit of it."

homecoming.text: He has corked the bottle and set it down on the slate, and he looks at your hand before he looks at you, the way he always has.
homecoming.note: Day 98, the epilogue: Aldous after the ending (one-time; per cindermoor_cradle_choice). The brazier laid for whoever comes down the stair (Day 47) is lit in the dark ending; Oriel's name; the seventh novice; the door-warden's answer to the Provost (Day 66).

home_lit.text: I felt it go. Two nights back. Like the Gull, the hand on the back of my neck. Only it was the whole sky had hold of me, and it didn't let go.
It's lit. And your hand's empty. ...It started with you, then. It would. It always starts with the hand.
You asked me once did I know you. I still don't. I'd think now neither do you.

home_released.text: It isn't lit. I'd have felt it. ...And your hand's empty.
There's nothing in the cradle to feed, and nobody in the room. It isn't worth lighting.
Something goes across his face that might have been a laugh, a long time ago.
'When the Spire's lit, or when it isn't worth lighting.' I wrote that to the Provost. I meant it for a door-warden's answer. A way of saying never.
Nothing in the cradle. Nine hundred years, and nothing in it. I'd not have believed I'd live to be glad of that.

home_dark.text: Still lit. I could see it in your hand from the breakwater, before I could see the boat.
The Spire's dark. At midwinter the ember goes round the ring, and every island chooses its own burning.
Chooses. ...Nine hundred years we chose for them, up the stair, and wrote it down after. Somebody'll have to show them how to write it. They'll do it better than we did.

choice.text: She signed the Long Book. "Oriel Sayre, High Keeper, who put it out."
Say nothing of the High Keeper.
The High Keeper's alive. She's sitting in a boat at the slips that never went out.
Say nothing of the High Keeper.

home_oriel.text: He says nothing for so long that a gull comes down on the end of the bench and goes again.
Thirty-one years I'd not say it. Names carry, in this fog. ...Let it carry, then.
She came down past the niche on the coldest night of every winter with a cup of something for the door-warden. Never said why. I never asked. That was the trouble with the pair of us: we never asked.
Signed it. Under you. ...Good. Somebody should be written down for what they saw.

home_oriel_boat.text: In a boat that never went out. ...That'll be her. She always did wait for the tide to make her mind up for her. So did I. We had that in common, at the end.

choice.text: The seventh novice on the east landing, with the light in their hands. It was me.
Let the stair be.

home_novice_told.text: He looks at your face, close, the way a man looks for a hook he's sure he put a coat on.
I still can't find you. Thirty-one years on that stair and I never lost a face off it, and I can't find yours. ...But I'll take your word over my eyes. My eyes were drunk a good deal of the time.
You went down past me with a light in your hands, and I let you. I never asked. ...I'm glad I never asked. That's a thing I didn't think I'd say about any of it.

home_brazier.text: He looks past you at the brazier by the Wrens' steps.
A door-warden keeps a hearth laid for whoever comes down the stair. I've kept that one laid since you asked me about the coal.
A door-warden keeps a hearth laid for whoever comes down the stair. I've never laid that one. Nobody was coming.

brazier_lit_ending.text: Nothing to light it with, now. It'll wait for midwinter and a coal down off the Spire, the old way. ...Except whoever goes up for it will have been asked. That's not the old way. That's better.

brazier_released.text: Nothing to light it with, now, and I'll not go looking. But somebody's been sitting at it. The step's warm of a morning, and it's not where I sit.
I leave it laid. A door-warden keeps a hearth for whoever comes down. They came down.

choice.text: Hold the ember to it.
Leave it laid, Brother. For midwinter.

brazier_dark_lit.text: Aldous gets up off the bench for the first time since you've known him, slowly, and goes ahead of you to the steps.
He lays it while you watch, with hands that know how: three sticks of driftwood crossed over a twist of dry wrack on the raked ash.
Your hand knows where to hold the ember: low, under the lip, where the draught comes in. The wrack catches, then the driftwood, and the Wrens' brazier burns for the first time since the Snuffing.
Thirty-one years on the stair, and all these on the step, and that's the first time anybody came down to it.
He holds his hands out over it. They're shaking, and then they aren't.

brazier_dark_left.text: For midwinter. ...Aye. Bring it round when you bring it round. It'll keep. It's kept this long.

home_crossing.text: I said I'd not get in a boat to be weighed by a chapter. Nobody's weighing, now, are they. ...I'll think on it. Don't tell Mara I said so.
He picks up the bottle, looks at it, and puts it under the bench with the empty one.

crossing_now.text: I told her I'd come when it's lit, or when it isn't worth lighting. A door-warden's answer. ...Well. It's one or the other.
Ask Oda what a Keeper pays. Twice, she'll say. Tell her I've got it.
Thornwold first, mind. There's a man on that ridge said he'd tell me a thing himself. I'd not make him come down a ladder for it.
crossing_now.note: Day 99: he knows Wynn lives (told on the east stair); the Mercy carries him there first.

crossing_now.text: He picks up the bottle, looks at it, and puts it under the bench with the empty one.

crossing_midwinter.text: I told her I'd come when it's lit, or when it isn't worth lighting. It's neither. It's worth lighting every winter, by somebody who's asked. That's not an answer I had.
I'll come at midwinter. With you, when you bring it round. Carrying nothing.
He picks up the bottle, looks at it, and puts it under the bench with the empty one.

after.text: I go up the walkway of an evening to where you can see it over the lofts. Every evening. Mara says I'll wear a groove.
Warm step again this morning. I've taken to saying good morning to it. Mara thinks I've gone soft. I went soft years ago; this is something else.
Keeps going, that fire. I feed it a stick of driftwood of a night. A door-warden keeps the hearth. Nobody said he had to keep it cold.
Still laid, and waiting for midwinter. So am I.

ridge.text: Aldous is on the plank seat in front of the lodge, his bag between his feet, the Ridge Light over his shoulder.
ridge.note: Day 99: Aldous on Thornwold's ridge after the two keepers' meeting.

ridge.text: You can see it from here, east. I came all this way to sit on a bench and look at a light with a man who doesn't talk. Best crossing I ever paid for. Twice.
The far end of the bench is warm of a night. He says good evening to it. I've started doing it too. We're a pair of old fools, and we're not cold.
I'll go on to Kindleby when Oda's going. The Provost's owed a door-warden in a room with the candles lit. Not yet, though. Not yet.
